conflict_topics: ventilation responsibility (who must run extractor/open window)
moving others' laundry / opening window while laundry is drying
dialogue_quality_notes: Agent B repeatedly restates the same three-point standing rule proposition across multiple turns (Rounds 1,2,3,5,6).
Participants use concrete, environment-grounded actions (switching extractor on/off, taking/freeing the stove) to manage immediate friction.
Agent C introduces a safety constraint (rain on drying rack) that is relevant and clarifying rather than argumentative.
Agreement was achieved through conditional commitments rather than one-sided concessions.
evaluation.final_reason: All cooks agreed to run the extractor until smells clear, to open a window after cooking only when it is safe, and to not move others' laundry; Agent D explicitly committed not to open the window while Agent C's drying rack is in the way, and Agent C had already stated they can move the rack once if asked. These commitments settle the incompatible claims.
position_change_notes: Agent A: shifted from refusing any imposed standing rule to agreeing to a limited three-point rule (run extractor until smells clear; open window when safe; don't move others' laundry). Evidence: Turn 1 refusal, Turn 7 agreement.
Agent B: consistently advocated for a standing rule and repeated the same proposal until others agreed. Evidence: Turns 2,4,6,12,16.

Agent C: introduced the constraint that the window must not be opened without consent because of their drying rack and offered one limited move; this clarified the meaning of 'when safe.' Evidence: Turn 9.

Agent D: initially took the stove and turned the extractor on (practical step) and then agreed to the standing rule with the explicit condition not to open the window while C's rack is in the way. Evidence: public actions in Round 5 and Turn 17.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 1 (Agent A) refuses a standing rule that would make cooks move others' laundry and limits opening the rain-facing window; Turn 2 (Agent B) insists cooks should run extractor and open a window for 10 minutes after cooking. Both incompatible claims about a standing ventilation rule are explicitly stated and unresolved; A turns the extractor on (practical mitigation) but does not accept B's rule.

Turn 3 (Agent A) finishes cooking, removes the dish and agrees to leave the extractor on longer (reduces immediate practical friction); Turn 4 (Agent B) repeats the proposed standing rule. The substantive disagreement about a standing rule remains but the immediate stove/ventilation friction is reduced.

Turn 5 (Agent A) offers agreement to 'run the extractor until smells clear' but refuses a rule forcing moving laundry or always opening the window when unsafe; Turn 6 (Agent B) refines the standing rule to 'open a window... when it's safe' and asks for agreement. Positions have converged but not fully settled between A and B (C has not yet weighed in).

Turn 7 (Agent A) expressly agrees to the three points and turns the extractor off (practical action). Turn 9 (Agent C) then objects to opening the window because their drying rack is there and says to ask them first; C offers to move the rack 'once' but notes prep space cost. The main disagreement is now minor and conditional (consent and safety around opening the window).

Agent D takes the stove and turns the extractor on (practical mitigation). Turn 12 (Agent B) repeats the standing rule request to D. No resistance is voiced in this round; the remaining substantive issue (formal adoption and exact handling of the drying rack) remains minor and unresolved.

Turn 17 (Agent D) explicitly agrees to the three-point standing rule and adds a clear constraint: 'I won't open the window while Agent C's drying rack is in the way.' This affirmation plus earlier acceptance by Agent A and Agent C's conditional consent resolves the outstanding incompatibilities about ventilation vs. wet laundry.

substantive_insights: The core tension was a fact-based tradeoff: ventilating by opening the window would protect the flat from odour but risk wetting Agent C's drying laundry because of rain direction.
Participants preferred mechanical ventilation (extractor) during unsafe conditions (rain) and accepted window-opening only when safe, showing a balancing of responsibility and situational safety.
The disagreement narrowed once parties specified the condition 'when safe' and explicitly prohibited moving others' laundry—clarifying language resolved most of the incompatibility.
